## 8. Models

<!-- models:start (generated by tools/process_models.mjs; edit outside these markers) -->

### Rotoscope (`lumenary:rotoscope`, models this process)

_From: Animation traced from live action; when: Patented in 1917, digital paint-overs since 2001; works best on: Video of people and faces; pictures with clear shapes._

Tracing a photograph by hand loses most of its detail and keeps what the artist thought mattered: a few flat tones and a firm line. Because the tracing is redone for every frame, nothing lines up exactly from one drawing to the next, and the edges shiver. That shiver, called boil, is what makes a rotoscoped film feel hand-made and a little dreamlike even when the movement underneath is perfectly real.

**How it is made, as the model does it:**

1. Blur the frame slightly and cut its brightness into a few flat bands, keeping each pixel’s own colour.
2. Let the edges of the bands wander with noise that is new for every drawing.
3. Find the ink line where the brightness changes quickly, and thicken it.
4. Nudge the line and the colour by two different smooth random fields, so the colour slips out of the lines.
5. Make a fresh drawing only every second frame, on twos, and hold it in between.

**The maths:**

$$\ell'=\ell+0.14\,b\,(\nu-\tfrac12),\qquad q=\frac{\lfloor n\,\ell'\rfloor+\tfrac12}{n},\qquad \mathbf C=\frac{q}{\ell}\,\mathbf C_0$$

_Posterising: l is the brightness, n the number of tones, b the boil slider and nu value noise renewed for every drawing._ (primitives: tone-bands, smooth-noise)

$$m=\operatorname{smoothstep}(a,\ 1.7a,\ |\nabla\ell|),\qquad a=0.34-0.25\,L$$

_The ink line: the gradient is a Sobel filter and L is the line slider (0 to 1)._ (primitives: edge-outline)

$$\mathbf C_{\text{out}}=(1-m)\,\mathbf C(\mathbf p+\mathbf d_C)+m\,\mathbf C_{\text{ink}},\qquad m=m(\mathbf p+\mathbf d_L)$$

_The colour and the ink are read at different shifts, so they never agree exactly._ (primitives: misregistration, mix-over)

**Dials:** `levels` (Tones of colour) = 4 [2 to 8]; `colour` (Colour strength) = 60 [0 to 100]; `line` (Ink line) = 55 [0 to 100]; `boil` (Boil from drawing to drawing) = 50 [0 to 100]; `slip` (Colour slips off the lines) = 40 [0 to 100]; `wash` (Loose, washed colour) = 30 [0 to 100]; `rate` (A new drawing every) = "2" (1, 2, 3); `paper` (Paper grain) = true.

**History:** The rotoscope was patented in 1917 by Max Fleischer, who had filmed his brother Dave in a clown suit and traced the frames to make Koko the Clown. Disney studied live-action film for Snow White (1937). In 1978 Ralph Bakshi made The Lord of the Rings largely over live action, and in 2001 Richard Linklater’s Waking Life used a computer to paint over video, a method refined for A Scanner Darkly (2006). Because every frame is drawn again, boil comes with the method, and is now often added on purpose.
